stimulus.text: The photograph shows a narrow alley between tall tenement buildings in New York City. Laundry hangs on lines overhead. Men stand in doorways and on a wooden balcony, and a man in the foreground holds a long stick. The alley floor is wet stone, with barrels at one side and a cart in the distance.
stimulus.source_note: Jacob A. Riis, “Bandits’ Roost, 59 1-2 Mulberry Street,” 1888. Photograph from the shared image pool; public domain.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jacob A. Riis, “Bandits’ Roost, 59 1-2 Mulberry Street” (1888); Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stem: Riis called this alley “Bandits’ Roost” and published the photograph in 1890. His purpose in publishing such photographs was most likely to do what?

options.text: Celebrate the beauty of tenement architecture
options.misconception: Reads a reform photograph as praise of architecture.

options.text: Show middle-class readers the crowded poor so they would demand reform
Advertise the alley as a place for tourists to visit
options.misconception: Turns a document of poverty into a travel advertisement.

options.text: Prove that immigrants preferred to live in alleys
options.misconception: Treats crowded housing as a free choice.

rationales.A: A dark, crowded alley is not shown as beautiful architecture. Riis showed it as a problem.
rationales.B: Riis published photographs of tenement life so that readers who had never seen the slums would see the crowding and demand change.
rationales.C: Nothing in the photograph advertises tourism. It documents poverty.
rationales.D: The photograph shows crowding, not a preference. No one chooses an alley for its own sake.
rationales.general:
Ask why a reformer publishes a photograph.
1. Riis photographed the poorest corners of the city.
2. His book reached middle-class readers who never saw those corners.
3. Seeing the crowding was meant to move readers to demand reform.
4. A photograph that only praised the buildings would need no reform.
Background: the books say Riis’s photographs drew attention to the plight of the poor.
Remember: a reformer’s photograph is an argument, so ask what change it argues for.
